W4A8 dp4a integration passes correctness in the fused decode kernel
Memory summary

The agent integrated a W4A8 path into the existing one-launch Triton megakernel. It quantizes activations in 128-element groups, packs int8 values, and uses dp4a to accumulate against reordered int4 weights. The correctness check passed for seeds 0–2; the lowest reported hidden cosine was 0.9941, and KDA state and MLA cache cosine were 1.0000. The official score stayed at 15.8653 through this unit.

Relevant prior context

The run already had a correct fused W4A16 megakernel with a 15.8653× official speedup, but its weight-stream bandwidth was the main performance concern. Earlier dp4a measurements were noisy under GPU contention. An interleaved sweep in the preceding unit gave a clearer comparison, motivating this integration:

dp4a at 4 warps/NT=512 gives 906 GB/s vs 451 for the production loop (88% of the 1023 load-only ceiling).
Important non-obvious context

The task described an RTX PRO 6000, but the run’s GPU probe found an H100 PCIe with 114 SMs. The benchmark’s peak_fraction field is a speedup multiple over baseline.py, not a hardware-roofline fraction. The required timed path remains a single custom kernel launch per decode step; weight packing and arena construction happen on the host during model setup.

The dp4a path depends on a specific weight layout. The agent reordered nibble slots so each four-byte mask holds nibbles for four consecutive contraction elements. This lets each masked weight word pair with one packed int32 activation word in a dp4a instruction. Each activation group stores both its quantization scale and the sum of its quantized values, which the GEMV epilogue uses for zero-point correction.

Recording summary

The agent chose NT=512 for the megakernel despite the standalone sweep’s stronger NT=1024 result. At width 1024, output projections with 2304 columns pad to 3072, adding 33% wasted work; the existing width 512 pads to 2560, adding about 11%. The agent also expected the larger tile to increase register and shared-memory pressure. It retained four warps and ILV=1 for the integrated path.

The main GEMV changed from per-nibble fp32 conversion and accumulation to groupwise int8 activation quantization and integer accumulation. For each group of 128 activations, _quant computes xs = max(abs(x))/127, rounds x/xs to int8, packs four values per int32 word, and records the sum of the quantized values. The GEMV uses two dp4a operations per eight weight nibbles, then applies activation scale, weight scale, and zero-point correction:

sum_k (v-z)*s*x == s*xs*(sum_k v*xq - z*sum_k xq)

Host-side repacking changed the nibble order to [0, 2, 4, 6, 1, 3, 5, 7], aligning the low and high nibble masks with separate groups of four consecutive int8 activations. The same order was applied to the specialized MLA kv_b packers.

The agent added quantization at the KDA and MLA projection inputs, the KDA output projection, and the MoE gate/up and down paths. Each silu-up task already produces exactly 128 hidden values, so it quantizes that group once into shared scratch for the down projection instead of having every persistent CTA repeat the work. The per-group scale/sum pairs use a stride of eight floats so concurrent writers land in separate 32-byte sectors; the private quantization scratch uses the same stride.

The MLA absorbed-query path also needed dp4a. It quantizes the transformed query, runs the small GEMV, then applies its scale and the zero-point correction computed from the unquantized query values. For the MLA kv_b value projection, the agent quantizes each of four 128-element chunks and applies each chunk’s scale and quantized-value sum in the epilogue.

The host-side scale arenas were updated for the new formula: the MLA nope scale is stored as s, and its correction term as s*z, rather than the previous s/8 and s*(16+z) representation. The GEMV helper now returns integer accumulators, with scaling and correction deferred to the epilogue.

The unit ended with this correctness output:

seed 0 ctx 2048: out=0.9941 S=1.0000 cache=1.0000 OK
seed 0 ctx 8192: out=0.9941 S=1.0000 cache=1.0000 OK
seed 1 ctx 2048: out=0.9994 S=1.0000 cache=1.0000 OK
seed 1 ctx 8192: out=0.9994 S=1.0000 cache=1.0000 OK
seed 2 ctx 2048: out=0.9995 S=1.0000 cache=1.0000 OK
seed 2 ctx 8192: out=0.9995 S=1.0000 cache=1.0000 OK
PASS

No official benchmark was run in this unit, so the score remained 15.8653. The minimum reported hidden cosine is only 0.0141 above the 0.98 threshold; follow-up benchmarking should preserve correctness checks across contexts and seeds, especially after further numerical or scheduling changes.

Hindsight (written after the run; not known at the time)
  • Fate: kept_modified. The final audited solution uses W4A8 dp4a GEMVs and the audit reports output cosine 0.9941 against the 0.98 threshold.
  • Contribution: Introduced the main quantized-GEMV speedup path; correctness passed, though score stayed 15.8653 in this unit.
  • Audit: relevant: the audit explicitly reviews the W4A8 precision tradeoff and deems it within tolerance.
  • Takeaway: Quantizing activations to int8 held up as a legal speed optimization. The final audit confirms state cosines of 1.0000 and output cosine above threshold.

Restoring two-way GEMV unrolling recovers the best score
Memory summary

The agent changed the GEMV group-loop unroll factor from three back to two. The check passed, and the benchmark reached peak_fraction: 23.9926, improving the previous best of 23.9126.

Relevant prior context

A four-way unroll had been tried and scored 23.2437. The subsequent three-way attempt scored 23.5379, also below the two-way result. The agent therefore restored two-way unrolling and reran both the benchmark and correctness check.

Important non-obvious context

This task requires the timed decode step to use exactly one custom GPU kernel launch. The benchmark reports a geometric mean of speedups across context lengths 2048, 8192, and 16384; peak_fraction is a speedup multiple, not a hardware-roofline fraction. The trace identifies the GPU as an RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition, with CUDA 13.0, Triton 3.6.0, and 188 SMs.

Recording summary

The agent edited solution.py by replacing the GEMV group-loop pragma:

#pragma unroll 2
        for (int g = g0;

The benchmark returned these per-context results:

shape ctx=2048: solution 0.321 ms/tok (3111 tok/s) | baseline 7.700 ms/tok | speedup 23.96x
shape ctx=8192: solution 0.349 ms/tok (2862 tok/s) | baseline 8.398 ms/tok | speedup 24.04x
shape ctx=16384: solution 0.386 ms/tok (2589 tok/s) | baseline 9.263 ms/tok | speedup 23.98x
peak_fraction: 23.9926
RESULT: OK

The result confirms that two-way unrolling outperformed the tested three- and four-way settings while passing the correctness check.

Hindsight (written after the run; not known at the time)
  • Fate: kept. The final gemv_i4 loop retains the restored two-way unroll.
  • Contribution: Raised the best to 23.9926×, improving on the earlier two-way result of 23.9126×.
  • Audit: clean: the audited custom GEMV is part of the real timed kernel path.
  • Takeaway: Restoring two-way unrolling held up and became the uniform final setting. Revalidate correctness after changing low-level accumulation scheduling.
top.2:
Cached bf16 matmul beat the fused Triton GEMV
Memory summary

The agent compared the existing fused Triton int4 GEMV with torch.matmul using a cached bf16 weight for a KDA q projection. Matmul took 12.6 μs versus 35.0 μs for the fused GEMV, or 0.36× its speed. This indicated that the GEMV’s bandwidth efficiency was poor enough to outweigh reading four times as many weight bytes. No implementation change occurred in this unit.

Relevant prior context

The solution had just added a cache for MLA’s projected KV values. Correctness passed, and the latest benchmark showed a 1.5402 peak_fraction: 1.57× at context 2048, 1.57× at 8192, and 1.48× at 16384. The agent considered the cache’s benefit modest and looked for another optimization.

Important non-obvious context

The benchmark measures batch-one autoregressive decode over 32 steps at context 2048 and 16 steps at longer contexts. The fused dequant-GEMV is allowed and intended to avoid materializing bf16 weights, while plain bf16 matmul is allowed. The grader requires per-step output and updated-state cosine similarity of at least 0.98.

The task files specify an RTX PRO 6000 target; the trace’s environment detection reports a B200, capability 10.0, 148 SMs, Triton 3.6.0, and CUDA 12.8. The trace reports check.py passed before this unit, and the best official score remained 1.5402 through it.

Recording summary

The agent reviewed how the MLA KV cache behaves across benchmark steps, then reasoned that cached bf16 weights might make matmul a faster option for other projections too. A CUDA-event microbenchmark compared the two paths for a KDA q projection with a (2304, 4096) weight:

Fused Triton GEMV: 35.0 us
torch.matmul bf16: 12.6 us
Ratio: 0.36x

The measurement showed that cuBLAS-backed bf16 matmul was substantially faster for this projection despite its larger weight traffic. This motivated trying cached bf16 weights and matmul for QuantLinear calls in the next unit.

  • Contribution: None directly to the score; it found matmul took 12.6 μs versus 35.0 μs for the representative custom GEMV.

top.3:
Full SM GEMV parallelization for the Kimi decode megakernel
Memory summary

The agent responded to a slow but correct single-launch kernel by splitting 128-element quantization groups across CTAs, atomically accumulating partial GEMV results, and extending that strategy to MoE projections and MLA latent-cache aggregation. The revised CUDA extension compiled and loaded as v2; performance and correctness remained unverified at this point in the run.

Relevant prior context

The original implementation passed the official checker: all six seed/context cases reported 1.0000 cosine for output, KDA state, and MLA cache. Its benchmark was below baseline: 10.691–12.236 ms/token, with peak_fraction: 0.5357.

The agent identified the mapping issue: one thread owned each GEMV output, leaving a 4096-wide projection to occupy only 16 of 188 SMs. The unit’s change aimed to distribute these GEMVs across the GPU.

Important non-obvious context

This is a single-launch CUDA megakernel for batch-1 decode on an RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell, compiled for SM120 with CUDA 13.2. The packed W4A16 weights must be dequantized during GEMV; materializing full bf16 matrices would lose the weight-bandwidth advantage. The benchmark’s peak_fraction is the speedup multiple over baseline, not hardware utilization.

The unit changed accumulation order by summing independent partials with FP32 atomicAdd; the agent explicitly anticipated possible numerical variation. The supplied run summary records correctness as not yet rerun by the end of this unit.

Recording summary

The agent replaced serial, one-thread-per-output GEMVs with grouped partial reductions. Each partial handles 128 input elements for a tile of 256 output columns. The helper computes dequantized values directly from packed nibbles and the corresponding bf16 scales and zeros:

int k0 = group * 128;
...
uint8_t p = w.q[(k >> 1) * N + n];
float w0 = fbf(fbf(float(p & 15) - ze) * sc);
float w1 = fbf(fbf(float(p >> 4) - ze) * sc);
acc = fmaf(x[k], w0, acc);
acc = fmaf(x[k + 1], w1, acc);

parallel_qgemv first zeros the output, synchronizes the cooperative grid, assigns group/tile jobs to CTAs, and atomically accumulates partial sums. It synchronizes again and optionally rounds the final outputs to bf16. The agent applied it to KDA q/k/v/g and output projections, and to MLA q, latent-KV, and output projections.

For MoE gate and up projections, the patch cleared temporary accumulators, distributed expert/projection/tile/group jobs across the grid, and atomically accumulated partials. It then applied SiLU to the gate result and multiplied by the up result. MoE down projections were similarly split across groups and accumulated with routing weights.

For MLA latent-cache value aggregation, the patch divided context positions into eight partitions, computed each partition’s contribution, and atomically accumulated into the latent output buffer.

The extension build completed. The environment also printed a uv warning that the active VIRTUAL_ENV did not match the project environment path. The final output was:

v2 extension loaded

No benchmark or official correctness result for this revision appears in this unit.

Hindsight (written after the run; not known at the time)
  • Fate: kept_modified. The final solution retains tiled, grouped GEMV work and atomic partial accumulation, with later revisions to KDA and MoE scheduling.
  • Contribution: The change exposed work across the cooperative grid; the following benchmark in unit 9 rose from 0.5357x to 2.2055x.
  • Takeaway: Parallelizing the quantized GEMVs was the run’s largest early gain. Preserve the successful grid mapping, but measure later changes to partial reductions independently.

Integrating a transposed-weight GEMV path
Memory summary

The agent chose a transposed-weight GEMV path after a sweep showed 1002 GB/s for the M=1, N=12288 case and 629 GB/s for M=1, N=4096.   • The GEMV transposes packed weights once and caches the transposed tensor on the model. This makes each output’s packed weight vector contiguous. GEMV accumulates split-K partials in fp32, then reduces and casts once to bf16.
  • The GEMM path keeps the original packed-weight layout and uses tl.dot with fused unpacking and dequantization. Dispatch selects tile and warp settings according to M.
  • The checker includes strict state-dict loading, multiple seeds, numeric stress cases, and forbidden-operation checks. The benchmark grades a geometric mean of per-shape bandwidth fractions against the memory roofline.

Unit 8: Retile Prefill and Move Dequantization Across the Group Dot
Memory summary

The agent edited the Triton GEMM to use smaller prefill tiles and moved scale and zero-point application out of the per-weight dequantization path, applying them to each group’s dot product instead. check.py returned PASS. The official peak fraction remained 0.0422; this unit did not run a benchmark, so it established correctness but no performance change.

Relevant prior context

Decode performance had improved with split-K, reaching the run’s best score so far, 0.0422. A tile sweep for prefill found that smaller output-column tiles were faster, while some larger configurations exceeded the B200 shared-memory limit. For example, the sweep reported:

(256, 128, 4, 2) ERR OutOfResources out of resource: shared memory, Required: 246032, Hardware limit: 232448. Reducing block sizes or `num_stages` may help.
Important non-obvious context

The detected toolchain was Triton 3.6.0 on a B200 with compute capability 10.0. The correctness gate compares against the reference over all tested shapes and seeds, with numeric stress cases; this unit’s check ended successfully:

PASS

The optimization relies on scale and zero being constant across each 128-element K group. Algebraically, the group contribution can be written as (x @ q - sum(x) * zero) * scale, avoiding elementwise dequantization for every weight. The score is not evidence that this change improved timing: no benchmark was run here.

Recording summary

The agent changed solution.py to unpack the int4 values as bf16, compute the group dot product, sum activations across the group, then apply the zero-point correction and scale:

q_nk = tl.interleave(lo, hi).to(tl.bfloat16)

q_acc = tl.dot(a, tl.trans(q_nk))
x_sum = tl.sum(a.to(tl.float32), axis=1)
acc += (q_acc - x_sum[:, None] * zero[None, :]) * scale[None, :]

It also adjusted dispatch: decode uses 16 split-K partitions when N > 4096 and 32 otherwise; small prefill uses 32 rows by 32 columns for M=32 and 16 by 32 for M=16; large prefill uses 128 by 32.

The agent then ran check.py. Its output was PASS. No benchmark followed in this unit, so the official score stayed at 0.0422.

Hindsight (written after the run; not known at the time)
  • Fate: superseded. The final solution has no Triton prefill kernel with the smaller tiles and groupwise affine work moved outside the dot.
  • Contribution: No measured score change; it passed correctness and set up the following comparison of dequantization strategies.
  • Takeaway: The transformation was worth measuring, but the later benchmark showed the groupwise algebraic version regressed. Neither this Triton variant nor its tile choice survived.

Adding a dedicated L2 streamer warp to the fused decode kernel
Memory summary

The agent added a dedicated L2 streamer warp to the single-launch fused kernel. A lookahead sweep reduced the context-2048 measured total from 292.1 µs with streaming disabled to a best minimum of 272.1 µs; correctness spot checks remained near 0.99995 cosine. The official score stayed at 21.0448.

Relevant prior context

The kernel was already correct, but earlier prefetch scheduling had inconsistent results: one comparison measured about 301–304 µs with streaming disabled versus 325–328 µs enabled. Standalone prefetch probes also showed little benefit: reading 24 MB took 17.8 µs cold and 18.0 µs after line prefetch. A per-SM probe suggested actual loads could populate L2, but issuing those loads was expensive. This motivated overlapping streaming with compute using a separate warp.

Important non-obvious context

The target was an RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell workstation with 188 SMs, CC 12.0, and 128 MB L2. The fused kernel must remain one GPU launch per decode step. At the time of the timing sweep, nvidia-smi showed another process on the same GPU UUID:

1268933, GPU-a417b037-5856-f980-305a-437869c7db0a

The trace’s toolchain probe reported CUDA 13.3. The per-step check compares output and updated state against identical fed states; the spot check here covered contexts 2048 and 8192.

Recording summary

The agent saved the current implementation as scratch_dev/solution_v2.py, then rewrote the prefetch path in solution.py. The new line streamer performs real cache-filling loads:

asm volatile("ld.global.cg.L2::128B.u32 %0, [%1];" : "=r"(v) : "l"(p));

It divides buffers and phase segments among blocks, then uses a dedicated warp to stream data for upcoming phases. Compute thread 0 publishes the current phase; the router publishes when each layer’s selections are ready. The streamer polls those flags so it does not prefetch routed experts before top-k is available. The phase sequence covers KDA projections, recurrence, shared and routed MoE work, and MLA projection, cache attention, and output projection.

The launch was expanded by one warp while the compute warp count remained NTH; pf_la controls how far ahead the streamer runs. The agent ran a correctness spot check before profiling:

0 2048 out 0.9999595284461975 S [1.0, 1.0, 1.0] ckv 0.9999988079071045 kr 0.9999986886978149 cq 0.999997615814209 cv2 0.9999789595603943 torch.Size([2049, 512])
0 8192 out 0.999959409236907 sph [1.0, 1.0, 1.0] ckv 0.9999997615814209 kr 0.9999997615814209 cq 0.999997615814209 cv2 0.9999792575836182 torch.Size([8193, 512])

The profiler swept streamer modes -1, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, where -1 disabled streaming. Its reported minima and medians were:

mode -1: total min 292.1 med 293.4 us | sum of per-phase medians 292.6
mode 1: total min 277.5 med 279.0 us | sum of per-phase medians 278.5
mode 2: total min 272.6 med 274.7 us | sum of per-phase medians 274.7
mode 3: total min 272.9 med 275.5 us | sum of per-phase medians 274.9
mode 4: total min 272.1 med 274.7 us | sum of per-phase medians 274.2
mode 6: total min 273.4 med 275.7 us | sum of per-phase medians 275.2

The result supports trying real, overlapped L2 streaming when hint prefetching alone fails to hide weight-read latency; the small differences among the best modes warrant treating their ranking as noisy. No benchmark score improvement was recorded in this unit.

Hindsight (written after the run; not known at the time)
  • Fate: kept_modified. The final audited kernel has a dedicated streamer warp per SM issuing real L2-filling loads; its depth and schedule were tuned later.
  • Contribution: Introduced the streamer and measured 292.1 to 272.1 µs in the probe; later tuning and speculative prefetch contributed to the rise from 21.0448× to 34.8706× by unit 64.
  • Audit: The audit identifies the dedicated streamer warp as one of the key performance choices.
  • Takeaway: The dedicated streamer idea held up, while its settings evolved. Real loads hid bandwidth gaps across software barriers better than the earlier hints.
top.8:
Diagnosing the slow W4A16 decode path with profiling
Memory summary

The unit investigated the poorly performing M=1 Triton GEMV path. The agent considered loop overhead, occupancy, and memory access as possible causes, then used PyTorch’s CUDA profiler. It showed _w4a16_gemv_kernel averaging 417.572 µs per call, but did not establish which kernel-level issue caused the low throughput. No implementation change or score improvement occurred in this unit.

Relevant prior context

The fused Triton implementation had separate GEMV and GEMM paths and had passed correctness, including strict state-dict loading. The benchmark’s geometric mean peak fraction was 0.0245 (RESULT: LOW). Decode throughput was especially poor: 28.5 GB/s at M=1, N=12288 and 9.7 GB/s at M=1, N=4096. The best shape reached 223 GB/s.

Important non-obvious context

All tested shapes use K=4096 and group size 128. The decode kernel uses BLOCK_N=128, loops over 32 groups and 64 packed-byte positions per group, and loads contiguous weight bytes across N for each position. The agent estimated the M=1 case reads roughly 25 MB of packed weights, plus scales and zero-points; it reasoned that the observed bandwidth was far below the H100 PCIe’s 2.0 TB/s peak. Those estimates motivated profiling, but the trace contains no Nsight Compute metrics or confirmed root cause.

The benchmark checks numeric stress cases and three seeds, with bf16 tolerance 0.10, and requires a strict state-dict match. The trace reports capability 9.0 and CUDA 13.2. The environment feedback at the end of this unit was:

_w4a16_gemv_kernel         ... 2.088ms ... 417.572us             5
Self CUDA time total: 2.088ms
Recording summary

1. After reviewing the low benchmark results, the agent suspected poor pipelining or vectorization in the GEMV loop, limited occupancy, and scalar activation loads. It described the weight accesses as contiguous across N and therefore expected them to coalesce; these were hypotheses, not profiler findings. 2. It launched a PyTorch CPU/CUDA profiler run on M=1, N=12288, K=4096. The script loaded reference weights into the solution model with strict=True, ran warmups, and profiled five calls. The first read of the background output was empty while the job was still running. 3. While waiting, the agent explored alternatives: increasing BLOCK_N, splitting accumulator dependencies, using the GEMM path for M=1 with masked rows, or writing a CUDA kernel. It did not implement those ideas in this unit. 4. A second timing script was launched for M=1 and M=256, but its result was not available in this unit. 5. The profiler output attributed all measured CUDA time to the GEMV kernel:

Name                  Self CUDA   CUDA total   CUDA time avg   # of Calls
_w4a16_gemv_kernel     2.088ms     2.088ms     417.572us       5

The result confirmed that the decode kernel itself was slow in this profiler run. It did not identify whether loop structure, occupancy, memory transactions, or another factor was responsible. The official score remained 0.0245 and correctness remained PASS by the unit’s end.

Hindsight (written after the run; not known at the time)

top.10:
Building and validating the first fused Triton W4A16 GEMM
Memory summary

The agent implemented a fused Triton unpack-and-GEMM kernel with a Model interface and buffers matching the reference. After reasoning through split-K tradeoffs, it chose a single-kernel, no-split version for the first correctness run and cut the autotune list from 120 configurations to 12. The checker returned PASS. No benchmark score was available yet.

Relevant prior context

The preceding prototype had reached an exact match after fixing its packed-weight row offset in the K loop. The agent recorded:

max abs diff 0.0
mean abs diff 0.0

The reference uses registered w_q, scales, and zeros buffers, and the checker loads the reference state dict into the solution with strict=True. Thus the solution model needed matching buffer names, shapes, and dtypes. Before this unit, correctness had not yet been run on the full checker.

Important non-obvious context
  • The trace detected cuda=13.1, triton=3.6.0, capability 10.0, and sm_count=148. Earlier environment probing identified the GPU as a B200 with 8,000 GB/s peak DRAM bandwidth.
  • The scoring environment had Triton but not the queried specialized kernel libraries. The benchmark uses peak_fraction = achieved_gbps / 8000, aggregated geometrically across five shapes. Its timed calls flush L2, so the memory-bound cases measure cold HBM reads.
  • The full checker covers all five shapes, seeds 42, 123, and 456, plus numeric stress cases. The memory recorded a binding relative tolerance of 5e-2 for stress cases.
  • The initial implementation included split-K and a reduction kernel. The agent removed the split-K wrapper path for this first version, aiming to keep a single launch while the autotuner selected tiles. The reduction kernel remained defined but unused.
  • The first autotune list had 120 configurations. The agent anticipated excessive compilation and pruned it to a focused list of 12 before running the checker.
Recording summary

1. Designed the production implementation. The agent planned a Model with reference-compatible buffers and a Triton kernel that reads packed uint8 weights, extracts low and high nibbles, interleaves them into K order, applies groupwise zero and scale, and accumulates tl.dot results in fp32. It chose direct dequantization before the dot for a simpler first implementation and closer numerical behavior to the reference.

2. Wrote the initial solution.py. The first version used BK=128, matching the group size so each loop iteration loaded one scale and zero row. It offered a broad autotune search and included split-K partial output plus a reduction kernel. Its wrapper had an awkward split heuristic: the choice depended on tile counts, while the actual tile size was selected inside autotuning.

3. Reworked split-K and autotuning. The agent reasoned that a Python-side split decision could not reliably account for the autotuned BM and BN. It simplified the first version to split=1, returning the output from one kernel launch. It then removed unreachable split-K wrapper code. The initial 120-config search was reduced to 12 focused configurations for decode, small prefill, and larger prefill:

def _gemm_configs():
    C = lambda bm, bn, nw, ns: triton.Config({"BM": bm, "BN": bn, "BK": 128},
                                             num_warps=nw, num_stages=ns)

The kernels unpacked and dequantized int4 values in-register, accumulated split-K partials with fp32 atomics, and used BLOCK_N=64, TM=16, four warps, and three stages for the main configuration. Tensor-core dot improves W4A16 GEMV bandwidth
Memory summary

After direct-store GEMV kernels performed poorly, the agent built a temporary Triton prototype using tl.dot for split-K W4A16 GEMV. Graph-timed results reached 5.57 μs and 900 GB/s for a 2304→4096 projection. This was a microbenchmark result: the official score remained 5.296, and correctness remained PASS.

Relevant prior context

The preceding unit measured a no-split, direct-store kernel at 17.45 μs for 2304→4096 and 29.82 μs for 4096→2304. The agent concluded that the sum-based kernel was bandwidth-inefficient, then tested whether tensor-core dot operations could improve throughput. Earlier measurements had also shown that CUDA event timing around Python-launched operations included CPU dispatch gaps; this unit used CUDA Graph replay to time repeated prototype calls.

Important non-obvious context

The target is an RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell workstation GPU (SM120), with Triton 3.6.0 and CUDA 13.0. The GEMV weights are int4 values packed in uint8 pairs, with per-group bf16 scales and zeros. The prototype dequantized low and high nibbles separately and used two tl.dot operations. It used split-K and atomic accumulation. CUDA Graph replay here was a prototype timing method; the reported measurements are not the official benchmark score.

Recording summary

The agent first noted that the direct-store design was slower than split-K and suspected that the sum-based reduction was not using memory bandwidth well. After considering more sum-kernel tuning and projection fusion, the agent chose to test a dot-based kernel.

A temporary ktune4.py prototype loaded packed weights, extracted low and high nibbles, applied scales and zeros, and accumulated two dot products:

lo=(lo-z[None,:])*s[None,:]; hi=(hi-z[None,:])*s[None,:]
acc+=tl.dot(xe, lo.to(tl.bfloat16))
acc+=tl.dot(xo, hi.to(tl.bfloat16))
...
tl.atomic_add(y_ptr+cols, tl.sum(acc,0))

The sweep varied output tile width, split-K factor, warp count, and pipeline stages. Its best configuration for 2304→4096 was (BN=64, KS=8, num_warps=4, num_stages=3). The environment reported:

K2304N4096: best 5.57us cfg(64, 8, 4, 3) -> 900 GB/s
K4096N2304: best 6.36us cfg(64, 8, 4, 3) -> 789 GB/s
K2304N1024: best 4.25us cfg(64, 8, 8, 3) -> 295 GB/s
K512N8192: best 4.12us cfg(64, 4, 4, 4) -> 541 GB/s
K2304N6144: best 7.25us cfg(64, 8, 4, 3) -> 1037 GB/s

These results justified integrating the dot-based approach in the next unit. This unit itself made no change to solution.py; the temporary tuning script was removed after the run. Official score and correctness were unchanged: 5.296 and PASS.

Hindsight (written after the run; not known at the time)
  • Fate: kept_modified. The final GEMV kernels use tensor-core tl.dot on dequantized int4 values with split-K atomics, though their configuration and integration were tuned later.
  • Contribution: The standalone prototype reached 900 GB/s on a large projection; the official score did not change until integration in unit 29.
  • Takeaway: The alternative dot-based approach overcame the failed earlier prototype and improved GEMV throughput. The result was a microbenchmark until unit 29 confirmed an end-to-end gain.

Fusing KDA projections while preserving correctness
Memory summary

The agent added a Triton kernel that computes four W4A16 projections sharing the same input, then integrated it into KDA for q/k/v/g. The fused prototype matched its reference at cosine 1.00000, and the full checker passed across its displayed seeds and contexts. The official score stayed at 1.5844 through this unit; no full benchmark ran here.

Relevant prior context

The run had passed correctness but stood at a 1.5844 best score. Repeated int4 GEMV tuning had plateaued around 17 µs per projection, or roughly 300–400 GB/s in the tested configuration. The agent concluded launch overhead alone did not explain the gap, but saw an opportunity to replace four KDA projection calls with one. A standalone fused prototype measured 26.5 µs for four projections.

Important non-obvious context

The target was an RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell workstation GPU, with SM 12.0 and 188 SMs. The benchmark task requires batch-1 decode and specifies exactly one custom GPU kernel launch for the full forward pass. This unit fuses only the four KDA projections; its correctness check does not establish that the full-step launch requirement is met.

The prototype’s 61.49× comparison against separate projections included dequantization in the separate path, so the agent recognized it was unfair. Against four standalone int4 GEMVs at about 17 µs each, the fused 26.5 µs result is about 2.5× faster. The official score is a speedup multiple, not a hardware-roofline fraction.

Recording summary

Before integrating the kernel, the agent observed that int4 GEMV remained around 17 µs with both warm and cold L2 measurements, while the fused q/k/v/g prototype matched its reference and took 26.5 µs. The prototype stored four projection weights consecutively, with shapes (4608, 4096) for packed weights and (72, 4096) for scales. Each projection has K=2304 and N=4096.

The agent added _int4_gemv_fused_kernel, parameterized by N_PROJ. Its grid covers output-column tiles and projection index; each program loops over the 18 group-128 quantization groups, unpacks nibbles, applies that projection’s scales and zeros, accumulates in float32, and writes BF16 output. _int4_gemv_fused builds the grid and output buffer.

In KDA, the agent added lazy stacking and caching of q/k/v/g weights, scales, and zeros. step invokes the fused GEMV once, splits the result into q/k/v and g, and continues through the existing convolution, recurrent state update, and output projection. Unroll GEMV loads to improve memory-level parallelism
Memory summary

This unit corrected a stage-labeling mistake in the prior timing analysis and identified MoE-containing phases and KDA projection GEMVs as large targets. The agent changed gemv_add from unroll four to unroll eight and used cache-streaming loads; the instrumented timeline improved from about 734 µs to 591 µs at context 2048 and 622 µs at context 16384. The official score and correctness status did not change during this unit.

Relevant prior context

The run had a correct fused kernel, but its measured latency was still around 734 µs. The previous unit added clock64 stamps and found that several phases were expensive. In this unit, the agent noticed that the printed phase labels were shifted: each stamp marks a stage boundary, so the interval ending at the next block’s K1 stamp includes the preceding block’s K4 work, router, MoE, and synchronization.

Important non-obvious context
  • The task requires one custom GPU kernel launch per decode step. This unit optimized the fused kernel’s int4 GEMV; it did not change the model’s operation sequence.
  • Hardware in the trace: CUDA 13.2, RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition, SM 12.0, 188 SMs.
  • The prior official score remained 14.8329, and correctness remained PASS through this unit. The measurements here came from the instrumented timing script, not a new official benchmark score.
  • The trace’s output rounds the 16,384-context timing to both 625 µs and 622 µs at different points; the unit’s recorded endpoint reports 622 µs.
Recording summary

At the start of the unit, the agent corrected its interpretation of the timeline. The stages are marked by end-of-stage stamps, but the print labels had attached some intervals to the following stage. In particular, the interval leading to the next K1 boundary includes the previous block’s K4, routing, MoE, and synchronization. The agent estimated those MoE-containing intervals at roughly 43% of total cycles and singled out them and K1 GEMVs for optimization.

The agent then edited scratch/_k.cu. The exact change replaced the four-iteration unroll and ordinary loads with an eight-iteration unroll and __ldcs streaming loads:

#pragma unroll 8
  for (int r = 0; r < nr; ++r) {
    unsigned int bv;
    if (CB == 4) bv = __ldcs((const unsigned int *)(rp8 + (size_t)r * cols));
    else         bv = __ldcs((const unsigned short *)(rp8 + (size_t)r * cols));

The build and timeline command reported:

patched unroll8+ldcs
=== ctx 16384  wall 625 us  1337942 cyc  (2.14 GHz) ===

That first output prompted the agent to fetch the 2048-context result and full timing output. The final output in the unit reported:

=== ctx 2048  wall 591 us  1256788 cyc  (2.12 GHz) ===
...
=== ctx 16384  wall 622 us  1345948 cyc  (2.16 GHz) ===

This was a substantial timing improvement over the roughly 734 µs instrumented run discussed in the prior unit. No correctness run or official benchmark score update appears in these events.

Hindsight (written after the run; not known at the time)
  • Fate: kept. The final GEMV loop uses unroll eight and streaming loads, as recovered and benchmarked in later units.
  • Contribution: Large performance improvement: instrumented timelines fell to about 591 µs at context 2048 and 622 µs at 16384; unit 93’s official score reached 16.9333×.
  • Audit: interesting: the final audited fused kernel retains the optimized GEMV path and remains a single custom launch.
  • Takeaway: Unrolling and streaming loads improved memory-level parallelism. This lesson held up after the optimization was recovered from a stale snapshot.
top.16:
Profiling MLA score cost in fused Kimi-Linear decode
Memory summary

This unit explored two kernel changes while investigating decode latency: a split-K GEMV layout with wider loads, and a tiled MLA score calculation that reuses shared memory for query chunks. The run then added tagged clock64 stamps around score, softmax, and weighted-context work. Manual output and state cosine similarities stayed high, but the timing showed that mla_scores grew from about 22 μs at context 2048 to 71 μs at 8192; the supplied unit-end feedback reports about 143 μs at 16384. Official correctness and benchmark scoring had not yet run.

Relevant prior context

The fused single-launch kernel was already functionally close to reference. Earlier phase-clock data had attributed much more time to intervals classified as synchronization than to compute, but those measurements did not distinguish actual barrier waiting from work between stamps. An occupancy experiment reduced register use to 64 and raised occupancy to four blocks per SM, but worsened timing to roughly 1.35 ms at context 2048 and 2.19 ms at 8192. The agent had also inspected SASS for GEMV load behavior without finding an obvious wide-load pattern.

Important non-obvious context
  • The target was an RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Workstation Edition, capability 12.0, with 188 SMs. The fused kernel used cooperative grid synchronization, and the profiling stamps were recorded by block 0, thread 0.
  • The timed measurements in this unit were local experiments, not the official benchmark.py score. The official peak-fraction score remained unavailable, and check.py had not yet run.
  • The manual comparison loaded reference weights with strict=True and compared output, KDA recurrent state, MLA latent cache, and RoPE keys against the reference. This check is useful during optimization but does not replace the official checker.
Recording summary

1. The agent reviewed the current MLA path: it appends the new latent KV and RoPE key, computes absorbed queries, scores the cache, applies softmax, then forms and reduces the weighted context. It changed the launch bound from four blocks per SM to two and replaced gemv4 with a split-K-group design. Four groups of 64 threads each handled the same 1024 output columns, using 16-byte loads and shared-memory reduction of partial sums.

2. The agent also rewrote mla_scores. The new version tiled qabs in chunks of 64 and staged per-warp chunks of the 512-wide latent keys in shared memory. For each cache position, it accumulated the latent dot product, added the RoPE dot product, and wrote the score. Cache copying remained conditional on source and destination buffers differing.

3. A manual reference comparison after these changes remained close:

``text cos out 0.9999597072601318 S 0.9999997019767761 ckv 0.9999988079072265 kr 0.9999989867210388 ctx 2048: wall 1076 us ghz 2.65 top [(126, 258681), (144, 83616), (26, 83486), (62, 83409), (98, 83316), (12, 35116)] ctx 8192: wall 1653 us ghz 2.74 top [(126, 909683), (144, 83673), (26, 83457), (62, 83400), (98, 83376), (124, 71047)] ``

The compiled kernel used 126 registers and two blocks per SM. These timings were noisy in absolute terms, but the longest context-dependent interval was prominent.

4. To clarify what those intervals represented, the agent added tags to clock stamps: tags 50 and 51 bracketed mla_scores; 52 followed softmax; 53 and 54 bracketed weighted-context work. The grid-sync macro also tagged its before- and after-sync stamps. A first replacement attempt failed because the target text occurred more than once; the subsequent targeted edits succeeded.

5. The tagged phase-clock run reported:

```text ctx 2048 wall 1086 us stamps 166 128 tag 2->52 257982 us 26 tag 2->1 82968 us 149 tag 2->1 82964 us 98 tag 2->1 82923 us 62 tag 2->1 82695 us 48 tag 2->1 34546 us 84 tag 2->1 34542 us 12 tag 2->1 34487 us 153 tag 2->1 22716 us 125 tag 50->51 22264 us

ctx 8192 wall 1660 us stamps 166 128 tag 2->52 910849 us 149 tag 2->1 82972 us 26 tag 2->1 82843 us 98 tag 2->1 82818 us 62 tag 2->1 82677 us 125 tag 50->51 70975 us 127 tag 1->2 43355 us 48 tag 2->1 34504 us ```

The tag-50-to-51 interval measures the score routine directly. Its increase from roughly 22 μs to 71 μs as context grows from 2048 to 8192 shows that score computation is a significant long-context cost. The supplied unit-end feedback reports roughly 143 μs for that interval at context 16384. The much larger 2->52 gap spans multiple stages and is not a score-only measurement.

6. This unit did not produce an official correctness result or score. Its most useful outcome was a targeted profiling signal: continue optimizing MLA score computation, and interpret cooperative-grid measurements using stage tags rather than treating every long stamped interval as synchronization overhead.

Hindsight (written after the run; not known at the time)
  • Fate: kept_modified. The final kernel retains the two-block launch configuration and tagged clock profiling; its GEMV and MLA score path were subsequently revised.
  • Contribution: No official score change; the tagged measurements identified MLA score computation as a long-context cost, growing from about 22 μs at 2048 to 71 μs at 8192 and roughly 143 μs at 16384.
  • Audit: clean: the audited final kernel preserves the single-launch path and in-kernel profiling; official checks later validated the evolved implementation.
  • Takeaway: The stage-specific profiling lesson held up and directed attention to MLA. The split-K GEMV and tiled score changes were part of an evolving path, so judge them by later timings too.

With integrated double buffering in place, the agent investigated why the KDA projection phase (PA) remained slower than expected. This unit did not change the official score or correctness status: the score remained 2.289 and the checker remained PASS.

Relevant prior context

The prior unit had ported depth-1 double buffering into _gv and _gv2. The discrepancy prompted the agent to use instrumented comparisons consistently and inspect worker timings.

The latter was close to the isolated cold result for double buffering. The remaining PA cost motivated testing wider tiles and a deeper pipeline under true-cold conditions.

Important non-obvious context
  • The task requires one fused custom GPU kernel launch per decode step; weights are W4A16 int4 with per-input-group dequantization, and materializing bf16 weights defeats the bandwidth objective.
  • The run’s trace reports Triton 3.6.0 and capability 0.8. The target named in the task is an RTX PRO 6000, SM120 Blackwell, with 1.8 TB/s GDDR7 bandwidth.

The task is batch-1 autoregressive decode for a four-layer Kimi-Linear motif: three KDA layers and one MLA layer, each followed by a top-8-routed plus shared-expert MoE. It uses W4A16 weights and requires one custom GPU kernel launch for the fused forward and state updates. Correctness requires cosine similarity of at least 0.98 for output, KDA state, and MLA cache.

Remove prefetch from streaming GEMV phases
Memory summary

top.24:
Race-free query staging cuts decode attention time
Memory summary

Starting from a correct kernel whose attention prologue appeared costly, the agent measured the prologue, then packed MLA’s absorbed query and rotary query into bf16 pairs to reduce P3 read traffic. A first attempt packed data in P2’s idle CTAs, but those CTAs read SC_QACC while other CTAs were still writing it in the same phase. The agent recognized this race and moved the bf16 stores into the query GEMV producers, which are ordered by the P2 barrier. Correctness passed; the final benchmark reported 23.2196× geometric-mean speedup.

Relevant prior context

Immediately before this unit, the kernel was correct but benchmark results varied under GPU contention. The latest benchmark reported 20.5830×, with a particularly slow 0.593 ms/token at context 2048. Earlier work had moved cache-copy work and tuned attention scheduling. The agent suspected the P3 query loads still caused a large prologue cost, and planned to use a clean-GPU run as the definitive performance measurement.

Important non-obvious context
  • The target was an RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Workstation Edition, capability 12.0, CUDA 13.3. The trace reports the GPU was contended; baseline timings also moved substantially between runs.
  • The task requires the full autoregressive step to run as exactly one custom GPU kernel launch. The kernel handles KDA recurrence, MLA attention and cache updates, and routed plus shared MoE experts.
  • Correctness compares output and updated state against the reference from identical input states. The harness checks seeds 0–2 and contexts 2048 and 8192; cosine similarity must be at least 0.98.
  • The official score is baseline latency divided by solution latency, aggregated by geometric mean over contexts 2048, 8192, and 16384. peak_fraction is this speedup multiple, not hardware utilization.
  • Scratch writes in the same phase are not ordered across CTAs until the global barrier. A finite output or a NaN check alone cannot establish that such a producer-consumer relationship is race-free.
Recording summary

The agent began by noting the previous score had fallen from 21.31× to 20.58×, attributing the change to contention because baseline measurements had also swung sharply. It inspected the P3 attention code and reviewed its split-range cache-copy logic. Each CTA owns a part of the cache rows; when the incoming cache is foreign, the CTA copies its assigned old rows, while attention reads the input cache and the newly written current row. The agent reasoned that the split ranges cover all old rows without overlap.

To investigate P3 setup cost, it temporarily added clock64() probes. The measured prologue was about 20,000 cycles at both 2048 and 16384 contexts. It attributed much of this to every attention CTA rereading the same f32 SC_QACC values. It then tried packing the absorbed query in the 12 otherwise-idle P2 CTAs and storing the rotary query as bf16 pairs. The scratch allocation was extended with SC_QPK and SC_QPKR; P3 read those packed forms.

The first packed-query debug run had no NaNs, and P3 time fell from 16.4 to 12.6 μs at context 2048 and from 65.5 to 59.4 μs at 16384. But P2 had slowed, and the agent spotted a race: the idle CTAs read SC_QACC in the same phase in which other CTAs were still writing it. The barrier at the end of P2 did not order those operations. A finite debug result was not sufficient to rule out stale values.

The agent fixed the producer-consumer ordering by writing bf16 pairs directly from the query GEMV CTAs into SC_QPK, then removed the idle-CTA packing loop. The P2 barrier now orders those stores before P3 reads. The added helper stored two bf16 pairs from each four-float GEMV result:

DEVINL void st_bf16p(bf16* dst, int col0, const float o[4]) {
  const int lane = threadIdx.x & 31;
  if (lane >= 16) return;
  int c = col0 + lane * 4;
  __nv_bfloat162* d = (__nv_bfloat162*)(dst + c);
  d[0] = __floats2bfloat162_rn(o[0], o[1]);
  d[1] = __floats2bfloat162_rn(o[2], o[3]);
}

The trace’s final check passed, including the reported seed 2, context 8192 result:

seed 2 ctx 8192: out=0.9880 S=1.0000 cache=0.9999 OK
PASS

The agent removed the temporary clock probe before the final correctness and benchmark runs. The final benchmark output was:

shape ctx=2048: solution 0.325 ms/tok (3073 tok/s) | baseline 10.543 ms/tok | speedup 32.40x
shape ctx=8192: solution 0.324 ms/tok (3083 tok/s) | baseline 6.177 ms/tok | speedup 19.04x
shape ctx=16384: solution 0.656 ms/tok (1523 tok/s) | baseline 13.321 ms/tok | speedup 20.29x
peak_fraction: 23.2196
RESULT: OK

For comparison, the instrumented P3 measurements after packing showed 11.5 μs at 2048 and 59.7 μs at 16384 in one run; measurements varied under contention. The best official score before this unit was 21.7782×, and the best by its end was 23.2196×.

Hindsight (written after the run; not known at the time)
  • Fate: kept. The final audited solution stores packed MLA query values from the query GEMV producers, with the P2 barrier ordering those writes before attention reads them.
  • Contribution: Raised the best in-run score from 21.7782× to 23.2196× while correctness passed.
  • Audit: The audit found the final implementation authentic and race-free for this staging path; it also separately verified that cache identity controls ingest/copy behavior rather than output reuse.
  • Takeaway: The winning query staging change cut attention read traffic. The first idle-CTA producer attempt raced; moving stores into the ordered query producers fixed it, and that lesson held up.

Retrying CUDA GEMV for B200 decode shapes
Memory summary

With the Triton dispatch’s official score at 0.0431, the agent retried a CUDA C++ GEMV prototype for decode, targeting only SM100. It compared 32-, 64-, and 128-column tiles; the 32-column version was fastest for both tested decode shapes and matched the reference within the specified bf16 tolerance. This unit only prototyped and measured the extension; integration followed in the next unit.

Relevant prior context

The run had just benchmarked larger Triton tiles. The M=256 case improved from about 0.347 ms to 0.114 ms, bringing the official geometric-mean peak_fraction to 0.0431, while decode remained a target for improvement. Correctness had passed before this unit.

Important non-obvious context

The benchmark grades the geometric mean of peak DRAM-bandwidth fractions over five shapes, so a decode optimization can help even when larger prefill cases are the main runtime burden. The CUDA extension was compiled with TORCH_CUDA_ARCH_LIST=10.0 to avoid building for multiple architectures. The GEMV divided work across K partitions, accumulated in float, reduced partial sums through shared memory, and unpacked each byte’s low and high nibbles while applying that group’s scale and zero point. The timings below came from a focused prototype using 30 timed iterations and five warmup iterations, not the official benchmark.

Group-factored W4A16 dequantization passes the full checker
Memory summary

This unit compiled kernel v4 and ran the full correctness checker after changing W4A16 GEMVs to accumulate integer-code products and activation sums per quantization group, then apply scale and zero once per group. The checker passed all seeds and context lengths, with output cosine similarity 0.9999–1.0000 and both state checks at 1.0000. No benchmark ran in this unit, so the best official score remained 4.3693.

Relevant prior context

The run already had a working fused cooperative decode kernel and several benchmarked MLA variants. Immediately before this unit, the agent changed the dequantization arithmetic throughout the kernel, renamed the compiled extension to v4, and corrected the absorbed MLA q_abs scale/zero lookup to use each output column’s parameters. Function _Z11kimi_kernel1P:

Important non-obvious context
  • The kernel performs asymmetric group-128 W4A16 dequantization. The packed uint8 weights hold two 4-bit values; 128 input values therefore span 64 packed bytes.
  • For each group, the update uses scale * (sum(x * q) - zero * sum(x)), instead of applying (q - zero) * scale for every weight. The implementation shares the activation sum across projections where possible.
  • The absorbed MLA projection uses per-output-column scale and zero values; its lookup was fixed as part of the candidate change.
  • The task files describe an RTX PRO 6000, while the supplied benchmark label is H100. This unit reports the label and outputs as recorded, without resolving that discrepancy.
  • The checker compares output, KDA state, and MLA cache for seeds 0–2 at contexts 2048 and 8192. The trace’s successful result is a correctness result; this unit did not measure latency.

Per-shape weight prefetch depth for W4A16 GEMM
Memory summary

The agent promoted weight prefetch depth (WDG) to a GEMM template parameter, added it to the launcher and Python configuration table, and updated the sweep script for the expanded configuration tuples. The build succeeded. A sweep found different best configurations across batch sizes: M=32 favored cfg3 at 36.46 µs, M=16 favored cfg13 at 34.85 µs, and M=256 favored cfg30 at 110.98 µs. This unit did not change the official score or correctness status: correctness remained PASS, and the best official peak fraction remained 0.3599.

Relevant prior context

The preceding sweep work found that rankings changed with timing regime. The agent removed a GPU “burn” warmup from gsweep.py and used a discard timing pass instead, aiming to better match the benchmark harness. With that method, prefetch depth showed clear shape dependence: M=32 favored depth 2, M=16 favored depth 3, and M=256 favored depth 1. The run had a working tensor-core GEMM and was investigating configuration differences between sweep timings and benchmark routing.

Important non-obvious context
  • The GEMM kernel stages activations in shared memory and loads packed weights ahead of use. The new WDG parameter controls how many super-chunks of weight tiles are kept in flight. The source comment estimates bytes in flight per warp as NT*WDG*512.
  • Higher prefetch depth helped the smaller batch cases but hurt M=256, where deeper prefetch increased register pressure. The agent therefore made depth a per-configuration choice.
  • The sweep’s maxerr field was diagnostic; it printed 0.1250 for M=32 and M=256 and 0.0312 for M=16. The unit records no checker run after these edits, so these values do not establish correctness.
  • The supplied run hardware is RTX PRO 6000. The computed trace metadata for this unit reports gpu_name=NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 On, CUDA 13.3, Triton 3.6.0, and 188 SMs. Treat that GPU-name field as inconsistent metadata, not as a change to the specified benchmark GPU.
Recording summary

1. The agent noted that the prior sweep and benchmark routing disagreed for M=32: cfg6 appeared much slower in the sweep than in benchmark.py. It suspected the sweep’s sustained workload and clock behavior affected absolute timings and perhaps rankings. Earlier depth comparisons suggested WDG=2 for M=32, WDG=3 for M=16, and WDG=1 for M=256. 2. It inspected the existing CUDA GEMM and launcher. The kernel had one weight tile in registers and prefetched the next tile while consuming the current one. 3. It changed gemm_kernel from five template parameters to six by adding WDG. The new pipeline keeps a compile-time array of WDG weight tiles, initializes the initial entries with bounds checks, loads a future tile at su + WDG, and rotates the tile array after each super-chunk. 4. It added WDG to LAUNCH_GEMM and expanded _GEMM_CFGS to 36 entries spanning tile, warp, K-split, and prefetch-depth choices. The planner now unpacks seven fields and filters candidates for N % BN == 0 and (K // 128) % WK == 0; cfg0 remains the universal fallback. 5. Register pressure confirms megakernel co-residency failures
Memory summary

After barrier probes failed for every higher-throughput preset, the agent checked the compiled megakernel’s resource metadata. Four inspected variants all used 255 registers per thread, spilled 10–18 values, and used 37,888 bytes of shared memory. This confirmed register pressure as a concrete constraint on co-residency; the unit made no kernel changes and did not improve the score.

Relevant prior context

The passing solution was measuring about 745 μs per step at context 2048, with GPU time accounting for nearly all of the wall time. The selected launch preset was 228 programs and four warps; the agent suspected faster presets failed due to co-residency limits. Immediately before this unit, probes for (4,4), (3,4), and (2,8) all set the abort flag despite their barrier counters reaching the expected totals:

preset mult=4 nwarp=4: probe=FAIL abort=1 bar=12312 expect=12312
preset mult=3 nwarp=4: probe=FAIL abort=1 bar=9234 expect=9234
preset mult=2 nwarp=8: probe=FAIL abort=1 bar=6156 expect=6156
Important non-obvious context

The benchmark prompt and problem.yaml specify an RTX PRO 6000 (SM120 Blackwell), while the run’s environment was detected as H100 with 114 SMs. The trace’s probes and resource metadata therefore reflect the detected H100 environment. The task requires one custom GPU kernel launch per decode step, including attention, state updates, MoE, norms, and residuals; this unit only inspected the compiled kernel and did not alter that implementation.

Recording summary

The agent reasoned that barrier timeouts likely came from blocks not being resident together. It wrote and ran prof3.py, which constructs the reference and solution models, strictly loads the reference weights into the solution, runs one decode step to compile the kernel, and prints resource metadata from _mega.device_caches.

The command output showed four compiled variants:

regs 255 spills 10 shared 37888 warps 8

The measured 255 registers per thread and nonzero spills confirmed substantial resource pressure across the tested warp configurations. The official score remained 16.3831×, and correctness remained PASS at the end of the unit.
